item.title: Government assessing options to revive southern Taveuni desalination plant – Cama

item.content:encoded:
This comes as more than 4,000 people in southern Taveuni continue to rely on rainwater and water tanks for their daily needs, with concerns raised over the desalination plant that has reportedly been non-operational for some time.

Families in these communities continue to struggle with access to a reliable water supply, while prolonged dry conditions are adding further pressure to their daily lives.

Helping Hand Taveuni Coordinator Simran Lata, who has been visiting affected communities and listening to residents' concerns, is questioning why the desalination plant remains non-operational and when people can expect a lasting solution to their water problems.

When questioned about the plant, Cama says the Ministry is aware of the concerns, and officials have been visiting the site to assess the existing infrastructure.

He says the Government is looking at which components can be upgraded and brought back into operation to improve water access for affected communities.

Cama says the Ministry is exploring ways to make use of the existing facilities rather than constructing an entirely new system, which could be more expensive.

However, no timeframe has been confirmed for when the desalination plant could become operational again.

Meanwhile, Lata is also raising concerns about poor road conditions in parts of southern Taveuni, where schoolchildren, farmers and other residents face daily difficulties travelling on pothole-ridden gravel roads.

She says dust from passing vehicles is also a concern for children walking along the roads, while residents are calling for speed humps and road signs to improve safety.

The concerns were referred to the Fiji Roads Authority, which responded that the roads in question do not fall under its jurisdiction.

When questioned about the road conditions, Cama says the Government will bring relevant agencies together as part of its emergency response to look into the issues affecting these communities.

He says he hopes the concerns can be addressed as soon as possible.

item.title: Six children with autism receive care and support at Nakasi daycare
item.description: Six children with autism are currently receiving care and support at Little Achievers Daycare and Learning Centre in Nakasi, with the centre working closely with the Frank Hilton Organisation to support their learning, development and individual needs. The centre's Director, Shivani Krishna says Frank Hilton has also recommended two children to the daycare, while three other children, together wit
item.content:encoded:
Six children with autism are currently receiving care and support at Little Achievers Daycare and Learning Centre in Nakasi, with the centre working closely with the Frank Hilton Organisation to support their learning, development and individual needs.

The centre's Director, Shivani Krishna says Frank Hilton has also recommended two children to the daycare, while three other children, together with their parents, are currently attending therapy sessions with the organisation to better understand and address their children's conditions.

Krishna says the centre is also supporting one child showing symptoms of ADHD and two children with speech delays who are making improvements.

She says the centre believes in providing children with different learning and developmental needs the opportunity to learn, interact and grow in a supportive environment.

The centre currently has 35 children aged between one-and-a-half and seven years, having started with just two students.

More than 20 children attend daily, with the centre providing daycare, tuition and after-school care.

Krishna says running the centre requires commitment, as she uses her personal income to purchase educational resources and other necessities for the children.

She says parents also contribute by providing toiletries, stationery and bedding to help meet the children's needs.

Krishna says children are like flowers who need proper care, guidance and support to grow into future leaders.

She also acknowledges the support of her husband, who works as the Facility Coordinator at Oceania Hospitals, saying his support helps her balance running the centre with raising their three sons.

She is also encouraging parents to teach their sons to take responsibility from an early age, just as they teach their daughters.

The centre also provides morning and afternoon snacks, as well as lunch when children do not have sufficient food.

Meanwhile, Minister for Children Sashi Kiran says the first five years of a child's life are crucial in shaping their values, behaviour, communication skills and future development.

During her visit to Little Achievers Daycare and Learning Centre for its World Children's Day celebration, Kiran says children's experiences from birth to five years help lay the foundation for the rest of their lives.

She says quality early childhood education and safe daycare facilities are particularly important for working parents, especially along the Suva-Nausori corridor.

Kiran says parents should have peace of mind knowing their children are being cared for by trained and qualified teachers who focus on value-based education.

She also highlights the importance of children from different ethnic backgrounds growing up, playing and learning together.

With schools expected to close early due to the ongoing drought and El Niño conditions, Kiran says parents will need to make arrangements to ensure their children remain safe and properly cared for while they continue with their work responsibilities.

Sh e urges parents to ensure children are left in the care of responsible family members or daycare facilities and are taught the right values .

Meanwhile, University of the South Pacific trainee teacher Anish Kumar, who has been working at the centre for one year, is encouraging more men to consider a career in early childhood education.

Kumar, a former police officer, says his experience dealing with child abuse cases influenced his decision to pursue a career working with children.

He says patience is essential when working with young children, particularly those with disabilities such as autism, and teachers must be willing to interact with children at their level.

Kumar says he was initially shy when he began his training as the only male student in his classroom but continued with his studies and completed his certificate and diploma.

He plans to pursue a bachelor's degree next year and hopes to establish his own daycare centre in the future.

Kumar says teaching and guidance must begin at home and continue into preschool, as the values children learn during their early years influence their behaviour and development throughout their lives.
